To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the binary fraction and mass-ratio distribution depend strongly on the range in primary mass, the selection of targets, and the pairing function; and that the pairing function is an important initial condition for star cluster simulations.

the mass ratio distribution and the binary fraction derived from observations or simulations depend on the pairing function used, the range of masses included, and whether the sample is mass-limited or mass-unlimited.

(i) the observed mass ratio distributions of binaries are not representative of the binary population; (ii) the observed binary fraction of a sample is a lower limit to the binary fraction of the whole population; and (iii), the binary fraction of a mass-limited binary survey is a lower limit on the true binary fraction of the population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interpretation of binary populations, which is a prerequisite for understanding the star formation process.
the question how to pair stars into binary systems and how to interpret the resulting binary properties.
the consequences of different pairing functions for interpreting observational data and simulations of star clusters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive statement about the pairing function.
the mass ratio distribution and the binary fraction of a sample of stars are not representative for the population as awhole.
the pairing function used to analyse the data should match the star formation scenario that is assumed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a random pairing of binary companions is not representative for the binary population.
the pairing function should not be chosen arbitrarily.

pairing algorithms that are based on a mass-limited selection of targets and that use a random pairing function, such as the method used by Sana et al. (2012) for their binary population study, will lead to a biased binary fraction, mass ratio distribution and mass ratio dependence on primary mass.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pairing functions should be carefully considered when comparing observational and numerical results.
the pairing function used to derive the mass ratio distribution and the binary fraction should always be stated explicitly, since these parameters are strongly dependent on the pairing function.
a careful analysis of the binary fraction and mass distribution in a sample is required to infer properties of the underlying binary population.
